The exact current marker is INTERVIEW-91-f051c6d187cd7054. The screen asks for JavaScript solve(intervals,interval): insert a closed interval into sorted, disjoint intervals, merging overlaps and touching endpoints, and return the result without stdin/stdout, imports, or exports.

Approach: scan left to right in three phases. Copy intervals whose end is strictly less than the new start; then merge intervals whose start is at most the current merged end, updating both bounds; finally append the merged interval and all remaining intervals.

Invariant: the output prefix is sorted, disjoint, and finalized; during merging, the working interval is exactly the union of the new interval and everything absorbed so far. Once the next start exceeds the merged end, sorted order guarantees that no later interval can overlap it.

Boundary cases include empty input, insertion before or after everything, insertion into a gap, containment in either direction, spanning multiple intervals, and zero-length intervals. Equal endpoints must merge—for example, [1,2] and [2,3] become [1,3]. The scan takes O(n) time and O(n) output space, with O(1) auxiliary space excluding the result.

Approach: use a JavaScript Map ordered from least to most recently used. For a successful get, record the value and move its entry to the end; for a miss, record -1 without changing recency. For put, delete any existing entry and insert the new value at the end; if capacity is exceeded, evict the first entry.

Invariant: after each operation, the Map contains at most capacity entries, stores each key’s latest value, and its order exactly represents recency. The result array contains one value per get, in operation order.

Boundary cases: empty operations return []; capacity 1 evicts on insertion of a different key; replacement puts refresh recency without increasing size; repeated misses leave recency unchanged. A stored value of -1 must be distinguished from a miss using Map.has, not the value itself.

Expected time: O(number of operations). Space: O(capacity + number of gets), including the returned results.

Approach: scan the nondecreasing times, computing Math.floor(time / windowMs). Track the current window and its accepted count; reset that count when the window changes. Accept an event only if the count is below limit, incrementing only on acceptance.

Invariant: the count equals the number of accepted events in the current window, and every processed event has its corresponding boolean. Sorted times mean a completed window is never revisited.

Boundary cases: empty times returns []; repeated timestamps share a quota; events exactly at a window boundary start a fresh quota; skipped windows require only one reset; limit = 0 rejects everything. These are fixed, not sliding, windows, so events immediately across a boundary have separate quotas. The screenshot does not specify parameter ranges; this approach assumes windowMs > 0 and a nonnegative integer limit.

Time: O(n). Auxiliary space: O(1), excluding the O(n) returned booleans.

This project is a token-bucket rate limiter, marked INTERVIEW-95-33d6a83015139fab. Its only supplied file, TASK.md, defines JavaScript solve(times,capacity,rate), returning one acceptance boolean per event.

The architecture is a single chronological scan tracking available tokens and the previous event time. Start with capacity tokens at time zero; before each event, refill by elapsed time × rate, capped at capacity, then accept and spend one token only if at least one is available. This takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, plus O(n) for the result; no imports, exports, or stdin/stdout are required.
